title: Compsassion Bodhisattvas
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching is that compassion is not just a virtue, but a fundamental necessity for human survival and peace. It is not limited to Buddhist or religious contexts, but can be found in various forms and expressions throughout history and culture. The Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, often depicted with multiple arms and faces, embodies the qualities of fierce compassion, humility, and wisdom. Through stories and examples from different traditions, the talk highlights the importance of cultivating compassion in our daily lives, including through practices like GRACE (Gathering Attention, Recalling Intention, Attuning to Self and Other, Considering what will serve, and Engaging ethically) and nonviolent communication, which can transform our relationships and society. Ultimately, the talk encourages listeners to embody compassion as a radical act of love that can set both ourselves and others free from suffering and violence.

sentences.text: So for the year 2018 we chose compassion as a theme for our sangha conversations and talks.
One famous proponent of compassion is Avalokiteshvara, so I thought tonight I would speak about Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion.
In other cultural settings we might say saint or archetype.
The goal of bodhisattvas is the universal enlightenment of all.
They are guides that remind us of specific noble approaches to our lives.
Bodhisattvas vow not to become buddhas until all beings have found liberation, and thus they continue to wander through space and time.
Heroic ideals of Mahayana Buddhism.
They can be awesome and they can be humble.
They can be heroes or our neighbors.
They are not restricted to appearing as Buddhists.
If you look, you will find them everywhere.
Avalokiteshvara was first known as the lord of what is seen.
She is also known as Kannon or [unclear: "Kansion"] or Kuan Yin, she who hears the cries of the world, or the perceiver of sounds.
Avalokiteshvara assumes many forms and takes on additional cultural elements as he or she travels to new countries and new times.
He's very fluid, and he is very fluid in his expression.
And yet in spite or maybe because of being fluid, there is a deep awareness of the true nature of beings and phenomena, of a way in which everything is right just as it is, just so.
Sometimes Avalokiteshvara is shown with a thousand arms.
Sometimes with eleven heads.
The eleven-faced representation is curious.
In addition to her face there are three smiling faces.
Three are scowling, for those who need stern guidance towards awakening.
And three have fangs to protect the faithful practitioner.
The head of Amitabha or Amida Buddha is said above all the others.
This is one story of how this happened.
The Bodhisattva had just finished saving all the beings of the realm of samsara.
That's the world we live in, the world of birth and death.
And she carried all the saved beings to the heavenly realm.
But when she looked back, she found that the world was already filled again with new suffering beings.
And her head split apart in [unclear: "grave"].
After this had happened ten times, Amida Buddha provided a new head to enable Kuan Yin to sustain her efforts.
So the eleven heads or aspects allow different mental perspectives and different attitudes with which to skillfully offer compassion.
The Dalai Lama said, "Compassion is not religious business.
It is human business.
It is not luxury.
It is essential for our own peace and mental stability.
It is essential for human survival."
In China it played out a little bit differently.
The Blue Cliff Record, case 89, shows how Kuan Yin responds.
*Yun Yang asked Dao Wu, "How does the Bodhisattva of great compassion use so many hands and eyes?"
Dao Wu said, "It is just like a person in the middle of the night reaching in search of a pillow."
Yun Yang said, "I understand."
Dao Wu said, "How do you understand it?"
Yun Yang said, "All over the body are hands and eyes."
Dao Wu said, "What you said is all right, but it is only 80% of it."
Yun Yang said, "I am like this, elder brother.
How do you understand it?"*
*Dao Wu said, "Throughout the body are hands and eyes."*
So Avalokiteshvara is not a dusty old Indian Bodhisattva who spreads sugary sweetness.
He may offer the other cheek at times, but his compassion at times also must be fierce.
His compassion may climb onto barricades or tear down walls.
What does she look like today?
What does he do?
I would like to introduce some most excellent Bodhisattvas: Roshi Joan Halifax, Shane Claiborne, Marshall Rosenberg, and Daniel Dennett.

Joan Halifax developed the GRACE model, which offers physicians, nurses and others working in stressful situations a simple and efficient way to open to the patient's experience, to stay centered in the presence of great suffering, and to develop the capacity to respond with compassion under all circumstances.
This model has been working so well that GRACE nowadays is used in education, corrections and other relationship-based services.
GRACE is easy to remember, which is important when we are in stressful situations.
It can help cultivate more compassion in our own life, or maybe it is a skillful way of expressing our compassion when we don't quite know how to step forward and say something or do something.
Recalling the elements of GRACE allows us to slow down, be more mindful and aware in the process of interacting with another.
Here's how to use the GRACE model.
G stands for gathering attention, focus, grounding, balance.
The R stands for recalling intention, the resource of motivation.
A stands for attuning to self and other.
C, considering what will serve.
And E, engaging, ethical enactment and ending.
I have asked Talus to attach a copy of a more expanded explanation of the GRACE model to the talk.
Thank you.
The next [unclear: "body, Satva"] Shane Claiborne wrote [unclear: "a literature for ordinary radicals"].
And this is a quote from that book.
*Peacemaking doesn't mean passivity.
It is the act of interrupting injustice without mirroring injustice.
The act of disarming evil without destroying the evildoer.
The act of finding a third way that is neither fight nor flight, but the careful, arduous pursuit of reconciliation and justice.
It is about a revolution of love that is big enough to set both the oppressed and the oppressor free.
Peacemaking is about being able to recognize in the face of the oppressed our own face and in the hands of the oppressors our own hands.*
Next [unclear: "body, Satva"], Marshall Rosenberg.
He was an American psychologist, mediator, peacemaker, author and teacher.
He developed in the 1960s the nonviolent communication system, a process for supporting partnership and resolving conflict.
It is based in people, in relationships and in society.

Nonviolent communication is based on the idea that all human beings have the capacity for compassion and only resort to violence or behavior that harms themselves and others when they do not recognize more effective strategies.
Human behavior stems from attempts to meet universal human needs.
Conflict arises when strategies for meeting needs clash.
NVC, nonviolent communication, proposes that people identify shared needs revealed by the thoughts and feelings that surround these needs, and collaborate to develop strategies that meet them.
The next Bodhisattva is the philosopher Daniel Dennett.
He offers a mindful way to engage with different points of view, more than a simple prescription of being kind.
He points out this is actually a sound psychological strategy that accomplishes one key thing: it transforms your opponent into an audience.
So he has specific instructions on how to engage with people with differing views.
One, you should attempt to re-express the differing position so clearly, vividly and fairly that the other person says, "Thanks, I wish I'd thought of putting it this way."
Two, you should list any points of agreement, especially if they are not matters of general or widespread agreement.
Third, you should mention what you have learned from the conversation.
Only then are you permitted to say as much as one word of rebuttal or criticism.
So what I took away from this is that compassion begins with the one thing we can actually change, and that is ourselves.
It doesn't end there.
It moves us from a place of reactivity, where we become easily disturbed by what others say and do, to a place of calmness and clarity.
Compassion is where great masters derive their strength.
It is the opposite of compassion which is truly costly.
The opposite of compassion represents the failure to see with clear eyes.
It is its own sort of mental prison.
Without compassion, we are the ones who suffer.
We are to be the peacemakers in a world riddled with violence.
That means interrupting violence with imagination on our streets, in our world, in our families.
Our aim should be to come at truth, not to conquer the opponent.
This way we don't lose arguments.
We gain new information and make new discoveries.
Of course, this isn't what happens most of the time when we argue, both online and offline.
But especially when we are sitting with our artillery of righteousness behind a keyboard, it's very comfortable to have a differing opinion.
So how about if we tried out one of these methods for one week and see what it feels like and what happens to our conversations?
And maybe if we like it for one week, we could extend the program a bit.
One week without snide remarks, personal attacks, tit for tat, one-upmanship.
Just pure radical compassion and kindness in every situation.
So what do you think?
Will you give it a shot?
